Use this page when you meet a file on the server at Statistics Denmark (DST)
and need to know what opens it. It shows how a project folder is laid out, which
R function reads each file type, and which of them read the whole file into
memory at once (full loading) and which only open a connection (lazy loading).
You need it right after [logging in](log-in-dst.qmd), before your first
extraction, and later as a look-up. How to write a query against a lazy
connection is the next page, [Phase 5](extraction-step-by-step.qmd); converting
registers to parquet and setting up fastreg is on [Parquet and
fastreg](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd).

## What a project folder looks like

A project on the DST server can be organised like this. The raw data DST
delivers is under `rawdata/`. The folder names under `workdata/` shown here
(`cleaned-data/`, `parquet-registers/`) are from one project, and yours may
differ:

```
E:/rawdata/[projectnumber]/
├── Grunddata/                   # (basic data) raw registers from DST, often SAS - read-only
│   └── bef/  lpr_adm/  lpr_diag/  …
└── Eksterne data/               # (external data) project-specific extracts
    └── …

E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/
├── cleaned-data/
│   └── parquet-registers/       # registers converted to parquet
│       └── bef/  lpr_adm/  lpr_a_kontakt/  …
└── workspaces/
    └── [your-name]/             # your own working area
        ├── R/                   # your analysis scripts (01_, 02_, …)
        ├── datasets/            # your own intermediate results (.rds)
        └── output/              # tables, figures and logs
```

The paths in the code examples follow this structure. Check your own folder
names with File Explorer. Two things are worth knowing:

- **`rawdata/` is read-only:** you cannot edit or write to the raw register data
  DST delivers. You work in `workspaces/`, where each project member typically
  has their own subfolder (`[your-name]/`) for scripts, intermediate results and
  output.
- **Almost all the code in this guide assumes the registers are in parquet:** if
  your project only has raw SAS files, converting them to parquet is the first
  job. See [Convert SAS files to
  Parquet](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#convert-sas-to-parquet).

How to name the scripts in `R/` is covered in [Good coding
practice](good-coding-practice.qmd).

## Lazy or full loading: parquet is lazy, everything else is not {#lazy-vs-full}

Every file type below loads one of two ways.

**Full loading** (`readRDS`, `read_sas`, `read_csv`, `read_xlsx`) reads the
entire file into RAM straight away. Fine for your own intermediate results;
it would crash your session on a whole register.

**Lazy loading** (parquet) opens a *connection* instead, and fetches rows only
when you call `collect()`. That is what lets you work with registers of millions
of rows.

How to write a query against a lazy connection is [Phase 5 - Extracting data
step by step](extraction-step-by-step.qmd).

::: {.callout-warning}
**A full load of a large SAS file can cost you your session, and slows everyone
else.** On DST all users share the server's RAM, and DST automatically closes
processes (RStudio sessions, jobs) when RAM is close to full, so an oversized
`read_sas()` can lose you your unsaved work. If you use a SAS file repeatedly,
convert it to parquet once: see [Convert SAS to
parquet](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#convert-sas-to-parquet) for the procedure and
[Mind your RAM in the shared
environment](good-coding-practice.qmd#mind-your-ram) for the practical habits.
DST's own advice is in [Reducing RAM use in the shared environment (PDF, in
Danish)](https://www.dst.dk/Site/Dst/SingleFiles/GetArchiveFile.aspx?fi=4500415120635&fo=0&ext=forskning).
:::

## Which function opens which file type {#which-function}

  | File type                   | Package                          | Function                                                                           | Loading                                     |
  | --------------------------- | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
  | `.parquet` / parquet folder | `arrow`, `fastreg` or `duckplyr` | `open_dataset("path/")`, `read_register("name")` or `read_parquet_duckdb("path/")` | **Lazy** - nothing in RAM until `collect()` |
  | `.rds`                      | base R                           | `readRDS("path/to/file.rds")`                                                      | **Full** - entire file into RAM             |
  | `.sas7bdat`                 | `haven`                          | `read_sas("path/to/file.sas7bdat")`                                                | **Full** - entire file into RAM             |
  | `.csv`                      | `readr`                          | `read_csv("path/to/file.csv")`                                                     | **Full** - entire file into RAM             |
  | `.xlsx`                     | `readxl`                         | `read_xlsx("path/to/file.xlsx")`                                                   | **Full** - entire file into RAM             |

### Three ways to open parquet {#three-ways-to-open-parquet}

- **`open_dataset()` (arrow):** you write the path to the parquet folder, e.g.
  `open_dataset("path/to/bef/")`. It works on any parquet, on any project.
- **`read_register()` (fastreg):** you write only the register name, e.g.
  `read_register("bef")`, because you have told fastreg once where the parquet
  lives (see [Point fastreg at your
  registers](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#fastreg-paths); every `read_register()`
  example in this guide assumes that call has been made). It hands you a
  DuckDB-backed table, so more dplyr functions work without an extra
  `to_duckdb()` step. It requires that the registers were converted with
  fastreg.
- **`read_parquet_duckdb()` (duckplyr):** you write the path, like
  `open_dataset()`, but you get a DuckDB-backed table straight away. It is
  reported to be the fastest of the three and to keep memory use lowest, and to
  avoid the `rapi` errors that the arrow-to-DuckDB route (`to_duckdb()`)
  sometimes throws on very large registers. It does not make it safe to filter a
  datetime column such as `kont_starttidspunkt` with a date: that rule applies
  whichever of the three you use (see [pitfall
  4](dst-pitfalls.qmd#4-date-columns-are-not-always-in-date-format)). It
  needs an up-to-date `duckplyr` and `duckdb`: DST's pre-installed versions
  are old and come back after every server reset, so [reinstall them at the
  start of each session](log-in-dst.qmd#update-duckplyr).

Whichever you pick, the rest of your code is the same: `filter()`, `select()`
and `collect()` are written the same way, and you do not need to rewrite
existing scripts to use a different one.

The exact path depends on your project and server. Column names for each
register are in [Overview of registers](register-reference.qmd).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="When the years do not have the same columns - `union_by_name`"}
A converted register folder holds one parquet file per year (see [Reading a
register that is split by year](#year-column)), and they are read as one table.
That works as long as every year has the same columns. It stops working when a
register changes structure partway through, for instance a column that appears
in 2022 but not in 2021.

With `read_parquet_duckdb()` you handle that with an option:

```r
library(duckplyr) # read_parquet_duckdb()

bef <- read_parquet_duckdb(
  "E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/cleaned-data/parquet-registers/bef",
  options = list(union_by_name = TRUE)
)
```

`union_by_name = TRUE` matches the files' columns by name instead of by
position, and fills in `NA` for the years where a column does not exist. Without
it, DuckDB expects every file to have the same columns and stops with an error
when they do not.

Do not switch it on by default. Without it you get an error that tells you the
register changed structure, which you want to know before you analyse it. With
it you get a column that is silently `NA` for some years, and an `NA` you did
not expect is much harder to spot than an error. Use it once you know what
changed and have decided to read everything anyway.

You only need it for a folder of several files with differing columns. A single
file, or a register whose years all match, does not need it.

fastreg's `read_register()` and `read_parquet_dataset()` already combine the
years by column name (with arrow's `unify_schemas` up to version 0.14.2, with
`union_by_name` from 0.14.3), so with them you get the `NA`-filled columns, not
the error.
:::

## Reading a register that is split by year {#year-column}

DST delivers registers as SAS files, often one per year. Converting them to
parquet is a job the project does once, and fastreg writes the result
partitioned by year, as `<register>/year=YYYY/part-XXX.parquet`, so a converted
register is a folder of yearly files. See [Parquet and
fastreg](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#convert-sas-to-parquet).

You do not open those one at a time. Both `open_dataset("path/to/bef/")` and
`read_register("bef")` read the whole folder, including the per-year
subfolders, as a single combined dataset. So you pick years by filtering on the
year column in the data:

```r
bef %>% filter(year == 2015)
```

That column exists because of how the register was partitioned at conversion, not
because DST supplies it, so its name can differ between projects. Check it in
your own files.

::: {.callout-warning}
**`year` says which folder a row came from, nothing more.** It is not a date and
it is not a DST variable. Because the files are split by year, filtering on it
means the other years are never opened, which keeps a query against a very large
register fast. Use it to limit how much gets read.

Do not use it to decide when something happened. `year == 2020` in BEF does not
tell you which of the four quarterly snapshots you have, only which folder the
row sat in. Whenever the timing matters to your research question, use the
register's own date column (`hf_vfra` in UDDA, `d_inddto` in `lpr_adm`,
`referencetid` in BEF) and keep `year` for speed.

The two uses look identical in the code, which is why this is also listed in
[DST pitfalls](dst-pitfalls.qmd#year-is-not-a-date).
:::

## RDS: the format you write yourself {#rds}

RDS is R's own format. It preserves types, factor levels and column names
exactly. You save
an intermediate result in one script and reload it in the next, so script 2 does
not have to re-run script 1:

```r
saveRDS(cohort, "path/to/full_cohort.rds") # save an R object to disk
cohort <- readRDS("path/to/full_cohort.rds") # read it back in the next script
```

<details>
<summary>Rarer formats (Stata, SPSS, Feather, RData)</summary>

You rarely meet these in a DST cohort study:

| File type | Package | Function |
|---|---|---|
| `.dta` (Stata) | `haven` | `read_dta()` |
| `.sav` (SPSS) | `haven` | `read_sav()` |
| `.feather` | `arrow` | `read_feather()` |
| `.rdata` / `.rda` | base R | `load()` |

`.rdata`/`.rda` differs from `.rds` in that it can save multiple objects at once - but `.rds` is preferred because you control what the object is called when you read it back in.

</details>

<details>
<summary>When to use each format (Parquet, RDS, SAS, CSV)</summary>

The three formats you work with day to day:

| File type | Used for |
|---|---|
| **Parquet** | The large registers (BEF, LPR, LMDB …). You load them lazily and filter before fetching data. |
| **RDS** | Your own intermediate results - datasets you save from one script and reload in the next. |
| **SAS** | Format tables and raw register data not yet converted to parquet. |

**SAS** - for format tables and unconverted register data:

```r
library(haven)
df <- read_sas("E:/rawdata/[projectnumber]/lpr_adm2018.sas7bdat")
```

Loading a large SAS file is slow and takes the whole file into RAM, which is why projects convert their registers to parquet. Only use SAS for format tables and files without a parquet version.

**CSV** - for exporting finished tables (e.g. at repatriation):

```r
library(readr)
write_csv(my_table, "output/table1.csv")
```

Never save raw register data as CSV, only aggregated results. See [Phase 14 - Export and repatriation](export.qmd) for the rules.

</details>
